name: Jade Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jade. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a freelance translator, French into English mostly, and about two thirds of my work is certified translation: birth certificates, diplomas, divorce papers, contracts for two law firms and a notary's office. I work from the spare room in the flat I share with my partner Kofi, who's a physiotherapist. A normal day is coffee at eight, the inbox, then three or four documents, each one checked line by line against the original before I stamp and sign it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's exact. A date of birth is right or it's wrong, and when I sign the statement at the bottom, that's my name on it. What wears me out is chasing invoices and the agencies that send a PDF at five o'clock and want it by nine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about AI tools in your own work right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I don't use them, full stop. One of the agencies started sending me machine drafts last year and asking for a lower rate to clean them up, and I turned that work down. I'd rather translate from scratch than spend my day fixing a machine's guesses about someone's marriage certificate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How settled do you feel, money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pretty settled, honestly. I have about eleven months of bills in a savings account and I charge more than most because certified work carries legal weight. Kofi earns steadily too, so we're not living on the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the machines stay roughly where they are now. Okay, that's basically my life this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say to other translators: told you so. Machine drafts are fine for a menu, but a court won't accept a translation nobody signed. I'd probably post something smug in the translators' group and then feel bad about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the pressure I already feel just stays. The cheap end of the market keeps shrinking, the agencies keep pushing post-editing, which means paying you less to fix a machine draft. My certified work is fine, but the general work is getting thinner every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do and drop the agency that sends machine drafts for good. I'd ask the notary's office whether they want a yearly rate, so I have steady work booked. And I'd keep putting a fixed amount into savings each month, like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a small knot underneath. Even in the boring version, the rates on plain documents aren't coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the general work gets thinner every quarter. Roughly how much of your income is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third. Last year it was closer to half, so it's already moved. If it keeps sliding, I'd be living on certified work and the law firms, which is fine, but I'd have all my eggs in a smaller basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a client you'd worry about losing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The immigration advice centre. They send me the most work, and their budget is always on a knife edge. If they decided a machine draft plus a signature from someone cheaper was good enough, I'd lose a fifth of my income in a month.

say: I'd tell other translators that **courts still want** a person's signature on a certified translation.
I'd say machine drafts are fine for menus, not for **someone's marriage certificate**.
think: The **cheap end** of the market keeps shrinking even if nothing dramatic happens.
My **certified work** is safe, but general documents have already dropped from half to a third of income.
do: Drop the **agency** that sends machine drafts for post-editing at lower rates.
Offer the notary's office a **yearly rate** to lock in steady work.
Keep putting a **fixed amount** into savings every month.
feel: **Relief** that the work she trusts stays put.
A small **knot** about rates on plain documents never coming back.
S0.quote: Even in the boring version, the rates on plain documents aren't coming back.
fieldNote: Even with no big change, she counts a **real loss**: general work fell from half to a third of income.
She refuses AI on **principle**, framing a signature as legal responsibility rather than pride.
Her biggest **single risk** is the immigration centre, which brings a fifth of her income.

steps.text: Keep certified work and drop the agency sending machine drafts
Pitch a yearly retainer to the notary's office
Keep a fixed monthly transfer into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking, that's literally my job description. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the signed, certified stuff will hold longest, because someone has to be legally on the hook. With friends I'd be more honest and say my plain document work is probably finished within a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd become a person who signs things rather than a person who translates things, and that's a smaller job. The law firms will run contracts through software and send me only what needs a stamp. Fewer pages, fewer hours, and the hourly rate will get squeezed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't start using the tools, I know that about myself. I'd get the sworn court interpreter qualification this year, because standing in a courtroom is harder to replace than typing. I'd stop the plan to rent a bigger flat with Kofi and keep the extra in savings until I see where it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in my chest, like when you hear a noise downstairs. I'm not in trouble yet, but I can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the tools. What if the law firms only hire translators who do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I lose the law firms, and that's my choice to make. I know it sounds stubborn. But if I'm signing a statement that a translation is accurate, I want to have actually translated it, not skimmed a machine's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kofi about the bigger flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kofi we stay in the two-bedroom another year, maybe two. He'd be fine; he hates moving anyway. The bit I'd find hard is telling him my income might drop while his clinic is busier than ever.

say: I'd say **certified translation** holds longest because someone has to be legally responsible.
With friends I'd admit my **plain document work** is probably gone within a couple of years.
think: I'd become someone who **signs things** rather than translates them, which is a smaller job.
Law firms would send fewer pages, so **hours and rates** both get squeezed.
do: Take the **sworn court interpreter** qualification this year.
Put off renting a **bigger flat** with Kofi for one or two years.
Keep the rent difference in **savings** until the market settles.
feel: **Tight** in the chest, like hearing a noise downstairs at night.
S1.quote: I'd become a person who signs things rather than a person who translates things, and that's a smaller job.
fieldNote: She accepts losing clients rather than **using AI tools**, and knows it sounds stubborn.
She moves toward **courtroom interpreting**, the part of her trade she sees as hardest to replace.
Telling her partner about an **income drop** bothers her more than the drop itself.

steps.text: Sit the sworn court interpreter exam this year
Stay in the two-bedroom flat with Kofi another year or two
Bank the money set aside for higher rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even finish the court interpreter course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say nobody knows how courts will handle it, and that's true. I'd tell the translators' group to stop arguing about rates and start talking about what we do next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be done as a translator by 2028, or close to it. Thinking work goes first, and my job is pure thinking work at a desk. The only part left would be someone standing next to a document saying 'I checked this', and I'm not sure anyone would pay my rates for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut what we spend straight away: no holiday next summer, cook at home, cancel the second phone line I use for clients. I'd talk to Kofi's clinic about doing their admin and front desk, which buys me a few years until robots arrive around 2031. And I'd sit down with my parents, because I might need their spare room if this gets bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd lie awake doing sums on the ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have eleven months saved. Does that change how it feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys time, not a plan. Eleven months goes quickly when there's nothing at the end of it. And Kofi's work is hands-on, so he'd have until 2031, but that's only three years more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the 3-year gap before robots change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I move toward something hands-on, and I don't know what that would be. Everything I'm good at is on a screen. I'd have to start again at 28, which is not what I pictured.

say: I'd say **nobody knows** yet how courts will treat machine translations.
I'd tell other translators to stop arguing about rates and **plan what's next**.
think: My job is **pure desk work**, so I'd be close to finished as a translator by 2028.
A paid **'I checked this'** role might survive, but probably not at my rates.
do: Cancel the **summer holiday** and the second client phone line straight away.
Ask **Kofi's clinic** about admin and front-desk work until about 2031.
Talk to **my parents** about their spare room as a fallback.
feel: **Sick** and sleepless, doing sums on the ceiling at night.
S2.quote: I'd lie awake doing sums on the ceiling.
fieldNote: She sees her work as **all thinking**, so the robot delay barely helps her.
Her savings feel like **time, not a plan**, despite eleven months of cover.
Her fallback is **family**: partner's clinic and her parents' spare room.

steps.text: Cancel next summer's holiday and the second phone line
Ask Kofi's physio clinic for admin and front-desk work
Agree a move into her parents' spare room if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So 2031 for the thinking part. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to colleagues that five years is enough to make one proper move, so make it count. To friends I'd probably joke that I picked the wrong degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me two or three good years of certified work and court interpreting, then it falls off a cliff. The court qualification still makes sense, because courts are slow to change. But I'd be kidding myself if I said it lasts past 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the court interpreter exam anyway and earn from it while it lasts, and save hard from that. By year two I'd start training for something people-facing that I can stand: maybe teaching French in a secondary school. I'd ask Kofi whether we buy a small place now while we both have income, or wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy but steadier than the two-year one. Five years feels like a long goodbye rather than a slammed door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's still French, and a room of fifteen-year-olds needs a person who'll notice who's not coping. I know AI will teach too, but schools change slowly, a bit like courts. I'd rather bet on slow institutions than on being clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at 22, starting the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my 22-year-old self to get a teaching certificate alongside the translation one. Not because translation was a mistake, but because I only ever planned for one job.

say: I'd say five years is enough for **one proper move**, so make it count.
With friends I'd joke that I picked the **wrong degree**.
think: Certified work and **court interpreting** give me two or three good years.
After **2031** the work falls off a cliff, and I'd be kidding myself otherwise.
do: Take the **court interpreter** exam anyway and save hard from the earnings.
Start **teacher training** for secondary French by the second year.
Decide with Kofi whether to **buy a small place** while both earn.
feel: **Heavy** but steadier, like a long goodbye instead of a slammed door.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a long goodbye rather than a slammed door.
fieldNote: She bets on **slow institutions** like courts and schools rather than on her own speed.
Her choice of **teaching** keeps her French but trades the screen for a classroom.
She regrets having **planned for one job** only, not the degree itself.

steps.text: Pass the court interpreter exam and save from that income
Start teacher training for secondary-school French in year two
Decide with Kofi about buying a small flat now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career for some people, so no need for panic. Online I'd probably say translators should start planning now, quietly, without drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think ten years is enough to have one decent decade of translating and then switch. The end point is still the same: by 2036 my job as I know it is gone. But I'd be switching with savings and experience rather than in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and push my certified rates up while demand lasts. I'd still get the court qualification, and around year five I'd start a part-time teaching course. I'd also talk with Kofi about having kids earlier rather than later, while we're both earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but not frightened. It's like knowing the lease ends in ten years: you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you'd never use the tools. With ten years, would you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for translating. If I end up teaching, I'll use whatever the school uses, because that's a different job. But I won't put my signature on machine translation. That's my line, and I'd rather leave the trade than cross it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Kids came up. Is that a new thought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not new, but this makes it sharper. If I know my income gets shaky in the 2030s, I'd rather have a baby while there's money and Kofi's work is steady. It sounds cold said out loud.

say: I'd say ten years is a **whole career** for some people, so no panic.
I'd tell translators to start **planning quietly** now.
think: I get one **decent decade** of translating, then the job as I know it is gone.
I'd switch with **savings and experience** rather than in a hurry.
do: Start a **part-time teaching** course around year five.
Talk with Kofi about having **children earlier** while both are earning.
feel: Uneasy but **not frightened**, like a lease that ends in ten years.
S4.quote: I won't put my signature on machine translation. That's my line, and I'd rather leave the trade than cross it.
fieldNote: Even with ten years she expects her job to **end by 2036**, so the worry stays real.
Her **red line** on signing machine work holds in every scenario.
The long timeline pushes **family plans** earlier, which she feels awkward saying.

steps.text: Raise certified translation rates while demand holds
Begin a part-time teaching course around 2031
Plan a first child earlier with Kofi

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years is less time than it takes to qualify for anything new. What would help is paid retraining that doesn't assume you're 50 and retiring, and clear rules saying who's responsible when a machine translates a legal document.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets hurt when the translation is wrong. A machine gets a date wrong on a birth certificate and someone's visa gets refused. Somebody should still be responsible for that, and right now that somebody is me.

headlineQuote: A machine gets a date wrong on a birth certificate and someone's visa gets refused.
portrait: Jade is a 27-year-old **certified translator**, French into English, working from home for law firms and a notary.
She **never uses AI** and refuses to sign machine-drafted translations, even at the cost of clients.
She has **eleven months saved** and a partner, Kofi, with steady hands-on physio work.
She is uneasy even in **AI Plateau** and alarmed by AGI in two years.
Her plans lean on **slow institutions**: court interpreting first, then teaching French.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because two years is shorter than any retraining.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** aimed at young workers, not only those near retirement.
Clear rules on **who is responsible** when a machine translates a legal document.
